etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English greten, from Old English grētan, from Proto-West Germanic *grōtijan, from Proto-Germanic *grōtijaną.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To welcome in a friendly manner, either in person or through another means such as writing.

quote.citation: c. 1593 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedy of Richard the Third: […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene i]:
quote.text: My lord, the mayor of London comes to greet you.

quote.citation: 1900, Charles W[addell] Chesnutt, chapter I, in The House Behind the Cedars, Boston, Mass.; New York, N.Y.: Houghton, Mifflin and Company […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Warwick observed, as they passed through the respectable quarter, that few people who met the girl greeted her, and that some others whom she passed at gates or doorways gave her no sign of recognition; from which he inferred that she was possibly a visitor in the town and not well acquainted.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To arrive at or reach, or meet.

quote.citation: 1707, [Joseph Addison], Rosamond. An Opera. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, Act I, scene 4:
quote.text: In vain the spring my senses greets.

quote.citation: 2009, Loren Long, Phil Bildner, Magic in the Outfield, page 47:
quote.text: Way deep in left field, where the carpet of green sloped upward to a terrace and greeted the thick line of trees, he reached out his glove.

quote.citation: 1725–1726, Homer, “(please specify the book or chapter of the Odyssey)”, in [William Broome, Elijah Fenton, Alexander Pope], transl., The Odyssey of Homer. […], London:  […]  Bernard Lintot, →OCLC:
quote.text: Fair on his feet the polish'd sandals shine,And thus he greets the master of the swine:

definitions.definition: (intransitive, archaic) To meet and give salutations.

quote.citation: c. 1588–1593 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Lamentable Tragedy of Titus Andronicus”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii], line 90:
quote.text: There greet in silence, as the dead are wont, And sleep in peace.

quote.citation: 1964 June 16, “All Eyes On Lema At U.S. Open This Week”, in The Indianapolis Star, volume 62, number 11, Indianapolis, Ind., page 22:
quote.text: Muggy heat—temperature in the 90s and high humidity—greeted early arrivals for the 72-hole, three-day test, rated the hardest and most important in the sport.

quote.citation: 1980, AA book of British Villages, Drive Publications Ltd, page 164:
quote.text: The first thing that greets you on entering the church is a notice asking you not to vex the goat, since it renders valuable service in keeping the churchyard tidy.

quote.citation: 2013 June 8, “The new masters and commanders”, in The Economist, volume 407, number 8839, page 52:
quote.text: From the ground, Colombo’s port does not look like much. Those entering it are greeted by wire fences, walls dating back to colonial times and security posts. For mariners leaving the port after lonely nights on the high seas, the delights of the B52 Night Club and Stallion Pub lie a stumble away.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English greet, grete (“great”).

From a blend of two Old English verbs, grētan, grǣtan (itself from Proto-West Germanic *grātan); and of Old English grēotan (itself from *greutan), both meaning "to weep, lament".

Possibly reinforced in Northern England and Scotland by Old Norse gráta, whence also Danish græde, Norwegian gråte, Swedish gråta, all meaning "to cry, to weep".

definitions.definition: (Scotland, Northern England) To weep; to cry.

quote.citation: 1933, Lewis Grassic Gibbon, Cloud Howe (A Scots Quair), Polygon, published 2006, page 312:
quote.text: And damn't! if he didn't take down her bit things and scone her so sore she grat like a bairn [...].

quote.citation: 2008, James Kelman, Kieron Smith, Boy, Penguin, published 2009, page 2:
quote.text: My maw went potty and started greeting.
